# Animals and humans

::: {.callout-warning}
## First draft

Written from `research/02-animals.yml` and not yet reviewed by a second reader.

Two limits are worth carrying through the chapter. Thirteen of its sources were
read as abstracts rather than as full text, and the Dscam1 material leans heavily
on one laboratory, which @sec-one-lab states where it matters. Several Dscam1
records are anchored on the authors' own preprints because no full text of the
journal version exists in this book's corpus.
:::

Almost every human gene is alternatively spliced, which on its own settles
nothing. A gene can make twenty transcripts that all do the same job, and a gene
can make two that do opposite jobs. The cases in this chapter are ones where
someone tied an isoform difference to a phenotype, because those are the cases
that carry weight.

They are also the cases where the evidence is thickest, which means they are
where disagreement shows up. Three of the examples below were presented as
settled in an earlier draft of this chapter and are presented as contested here,
because reading further into each one turned up a primary paper pointing the
other way. That pattern is worth noticing in its own right. An isoform story
told from reviews tends to be tidier than the same story told from the
experiments.

## Dscam1: diversity by combination {#sec-dscam}

*Drosophila* *Dscam1* is the most extreme example available, and the most
thoroughly dissected.

The architecture multiplies rather than adds, because three clusters of mutually
exclusive exons hold 12, 48 and 33 variants and splicing takes exactly one from
each. The combinations give 19,008 ectodomains, and an alternative transmembrane
exon doubles that to the 38,016 usually quoted [@dong2023dscamscreen].

![Three mutually exclusive exon clusters and one alternative transmembrane exon
generate the *Dscam1* repertoire. A single neuron uses a small, probabilistically
drawn slice of it.](../figures/dscam-combinatorics.svg){#fig-dscam width=100%}

The arithmetic deserves the space because the repertoire size is a functional
specification. Not, as it is usually quoted, a curiosity about how far
splicing can be pushed. Each Dscam1 ectodomain binds homophilically with
near-absolute specificity, recognising itself and barely touching the others
[@dscam2004homophilicbinding].
That property is what makes an isoform usable as a cell-surface identity label,
and the repertoire size sets how many distinguishable labels exist.

Neurons use the label to repel their own branches. Sister dendrites of one
neuron carry matching isoforms, recognise each other and turn away. Branches
of different neurons pass without incident. Recognition happens in the variable
ectodomain, but the cytoplasmic tail does the repelling
[@dscam2007dendriteselfavoidance].

Self-avoidance requires a neuron's isoform set to be *distinctive* and not to be
any *particular* set. The expression data match:
R3/R4 photoreceptors express on the order of 14 to 50 distinct isoform mRNAs
each [@dscam2004stochasticbiased], a vanishing slice of the repertoire. The
repertoire exists to make collisions between unrelated neurons unlikely, not to
assign meanings to individual isoforms.

That picture needs one qualification, because the draws are not independent
between cells. In situ detection of individual variants from all three clusters
found neighbouring neuroblasts carrying the same variant, along with the neurons
descended from them [@liu2020dscamcolumns]. A lineage therefore shares part of
its label, which makes the collision probability between two nearby neurons
higher than independent sampling from the repertoire would imply.

### One exon from each cluster, by geometry rather than by choice

Mutual exclusivity is the part of this system most often stated and least often
explained. It is not a decision taken by a regulator. It is a geometric
consequence of how the RNA folds.

A single intronic docking site pairs with the selector sequence lying upstream
of one variable exon at a time, which physically presents that exon, and no
other, to the upstream constitutive exon [@dscam2005dockingselector]. The direct
test of that model used minigene constructs built to mimic the loop the pairing
creates. Only the variable exon lying immediately outside the loop was spliced
in, and every other was silenced [@wang2012dscamlcr]. Exclusivity on this
account is a matter of what the splicing machinery can reach.

Two genome-level experiments support the same mechanism. Mutating the selector
sequence in front of a single exon 6 variant in the fly reduced that variant's
use and left every other exon 6 variant unchanged, so a selector acts only on
the exon it precedes [@dong2022dscambalancer]. A second and separate intronic
pairing holds down the exon 6 variants nearest the docking site, with
suppression strongest for the closest exons [@dong2022dscambalancer].

Timing fits a mechanism that works on the folded molecule rather than on the
emerging one. Introns around the variable clusters persist in newly made
transcripts while constitutive introns have already gone, so variable exon
splicing is substantially the slower process [@dong2026dscamrnastructures].

Two findings keep this from being the whole story. Fly nulls for the
non-canonical SR-related protein Srrm234 lose inclusion of many exon 9 variants,
with compensating gains at a few, so a trans-acting protein does shape the
outcome [@ustaoglu2019dscamsrrm234]. The same group disputes the pairing model
for that cluster, reporting that an inspection of the aligned cluster found no
conserved intronic element in front of every variable exon that could pair with
the proposed docking site [@ustaoglu2019dscamsrrm234]. The mechanism is
therefore well established for exon 6 and argued over for exon 9. An earlier
draft of this chapter asserted one clean mechanism for all three clusters.

### A count for dendrites, identities for axons

Two experiments take this from correlation to requirement.

Alleles cutting the maximum repertoire from 38,016 to 22,176 still produced
specific connectivity defects in mechanosensory neurons
[@dscam2006diversityrequired], which puts the number itself under selection.

A CRISPR deletion series spanning 396 to 18,612 possible ectodomains then showed
there is no single requirement to measure. Dendrite self/non-self discrimination
saturated near 2,000 isoforms and was indifferent to which cluster supplied
them. Axon patterning needed far more, and depended on which clusters were
present [@dong2023dscamscreen].

Diversity does two jobs in two currencies, since self/non-self discrimination
needs a sufficient count while axon patterning needs particular identities.

Pushing the repertoire lower makes the second job fail outright. Flies left with
one exon 6 variant, giving 396 possible ectodomains, or one exon 9 variant,
giving 576, had mushroom body defects at 64 to 100 per cent penetrance. Flies
left with one exon 4 variant and 1,584 ectodomains had them at 0 to 8 per cent
[@dong2022selfavoidance]. At those smallest repertoires a single neuron could
not reliably send its two sister branches into different lobes. Segregation
failed about as often as in flies with no Dscam1 at all
[@dong2022selfavoidance].

Two things about that experiment complicate the straightforward reading. The
reduced repertoires produced two classes of defect that a self-avoidance account
does not predict, truncated lobes and simultaneous thinning of both lobes.
Together those made up 10 to 48 per cent of defects in most single-variant
mutants [@dong2022selfavoidance]. And halving the amount of Dscam1 protein
rescued much of the damage, lifting survival to adulthood from 2 to 55 per cent
in homozygotes to 40 to 79 per cent when the same allele was placed opposite a
null [@dong2022selfavoidance]. A phenotype that improves when protein is removed
is hard to describe purely as a shortage of labels.

### Changing usage bias alone disrupts wiring

Isoform usage is skewed, and the skew does work.

The experiment that shows it was built so that usage distribution is the only
variable that moves. Both docking-site deletion alleles encode the same number
of possible isoforms as wild type and express the same overall amount of Dscam1
protein [@dscam2021splicingbias]. Deleting the exon 9 docking site then left up
to 20 per cent of mutant adult brains with defective mushroom body lobes,
against none in wild type [@dscam2021splicingbias]. The equivalent deletion at
exon 4 rarely did damage, with defects in roughly 2 per cent of brain
hemispheres. The requirement for a particular usage distribution is specific to
some clusters rather than general [@dscam2021splicingbias].

What the deletion does to usage is redistribution rather than loss. Of the 33
exon 9 variants, 19 were used significantly more than in wild type and five
significantly less [@dscam2021splicingbias]. How much a given variant gained or
lost was predicted better by base-pairing strength and looping distance taken
together than by either alone, which is what a pairing-based mechanism requires
[@dscam2021splicingbias].

The damage spares the function the repertoire is supposed to underwrite. In
single-cell clones carrying the exon 9 deletion, sister branches of one neuron
still never crossed or bundled [@dscam2021splicingbias]. Shifting the
distribution damaged wiring without breaking self-recognition.

### The resolution rests on one laboratory {#sec-one-lab}

The result above creates a problem for the standard account, and those authors
say so themselves. Strong and reproducible splicing bias is hard to reconcile
with a pure self-avoidance model, because heavy bias restricts access to the
diversity self-avoidance is supposed to exploit [@dscam2021splicingbias].

Their proposed resolution splits the job in two. Isoform number underwrites
self-avoidance, while a reproducible usage skew suits recognition and synaptic
choice by particular isoforms, which self-avoidance cannot use
[@dscam2021splicingbias].

That resolution is coherent and it is close to unreplicated. Of the sources
behind this section, the great majority come from one laboratory. That includes
every record challenging the self-avoidance account. A search of this book's
corpus for independent tests found one primary study from another group.
Knocking Dscam1 down in LC4 visual interneurons left dendrite length, branching,
coverage and spacing indistinguishable from control
[@wilhelm2022dscamneurontypes]. That agrees Dscam1 does something beyond
self-avoidance, and it does not test the bias claim.

So the honest summary is that one group has produced a careful argument that
usage distribution matters independently of repertoire size. Nobody else in this
corpus has tried to reproduce that argument. The argument is reported here as
theirs.

### Dscam1 diversity and surviving infection

The repertoire has a dimension outside the nervous system, and the evidence
there points two ways as well.

After ten days of *Metarhizium robertsii* infection, 12 per cent of flies
carrying a large exon 6 cluster deletion survived, against 71 per cent of wild
type, with no difference between the uninfected controls of either genotype
[@dong2025dscamfitness]. That is a large effect for a gene usually discussed as
a wiring molecule.

It does not follow that the immune system reads isoform identity the way neurons
do. After live *Escherichia coli* exposure, adult flies showed no statistically
significant change in the relative use of variants in any of the three clusters
[@armitage2014dscambacterial]. Diversity mattering for survival and usage
shifting on challenge are different claims, and only the first has support here.

### Clustered protocadherins reach the same end by other means

Vertebrates have no Dscam1 repertoire, and they have something that does a
similar job. The parallel is worth drawing carefully, because it is functional
rather than structural.

The two families share none of their protein architecture, yet both make many
isoforms at one locus, express them stochastically and combinatorially, and bind
homophilically [@lefebvre2012pcdhselfavoidance]. The mechanism differs at the
first step: clustered protocadherins depend on stochastic promoter activity
rather than on splice-site competition within one pre-mRNA
[@dscam2021splicingbias]. Expression in those cells is also allele-specific. Of
18 Pcdh-beta transcripts reliably detected in single mouse Purkinje cells, 17
came from one allele only, while a control gene was biallelic in every cell
[@hirano2012pcdhbetasingleneuron].

Where the parallel holds least is in what diversity buys. In mouse starburst
amacrine cells, deleting either of two groups of gamma-protocadherin variable
exons left dendritic self-avoidance intact. Replacing all 22 isoforms with
either one of two single isoforms restored it, which led those authors to
conclude that no isoform is necessary and one is enough
[@lefebvre2012pcdhselfavoidance]. The repertoire instead buys discrimination
between cells. When every starburst amacrine cell carried the same single
isoform, dendrites of neighbouring cells began avoiding each other instead of
overlapping as they normally do [@lefebvre2012pcdhselfavoidance].

Two later results qualify the "one is enough" conclusion. Starburst amacrine
cells left with gamma-C4 as their only gamma-protocadherin failed at
self-avoidance, unlike cells left with other single isoforms. The repertoire
contains at least one member that is not interchangeable
[@mcleod2025pcdhgc4]. And recognition needs the proteins to pair sideways within
one membrane as well as across the gap between two. Cells carrying matched plus
mismatched isoforms stayed apart, while deleting the domain that mediates the
sideways pairing made the same mismatched combinations adhere indiscriminately
[@wiseglass2024pcdhcis]. Dscam1 has no counterpart to that step, so the two
systems are least alike exactly where the recognition happens.

## Sex determination in Drosophila: a chain of splice choices {#sec-sexdet-fly}

*Dscam1* uses splicing to generate variety, while the *Drosophila*
sex-determination cascade uses it to make a decision. That cascade remains
the cleanest example of a splicing switch running a developmental programme.

The cascade is a chain of splice choices. Female Sex-lethal binds the
*transformer* transcript at or near its non-sex-specific 3' acceptor, forcing use
of the downstream female-productive acceptor [@sxl1990trasplicesite]. At the
bottom of the chain, Tra and Tra2 act positively, recruiting SR-family factors to
an element downstream of the female-specific 3' splice site of *doublesex*, and
that complex commits the pre-mRNA [@dsx1993spliceenhancercomplex]. That set of
proteins is sufficient for the female pattern rather than merely associated with
it. The individual SR proteins differ substantially in how well they join the
committed complex [@dsx1993spliceenhancercomplex].

*doublesex* also supplies the cleanest case anywhere of two isoforms doing
opposite things. The female product represses male differentiation, and the
male product represses female differentiation. Both are functional products of
the same primary transcript [@dsx1989sexspecificpolypeptides]. The two products
come from one primary transcript processed two ways at once, since the
sex-specific messages differ by alternative splicing and alternative
polyadenylation together, sharing a common 5' end and three common exons while
differing in their 3' exons [@dsx1989sexspecificpolypeptides].

### Sex-lethal blocks a site rather than activating one

The top of the cascade works by subtraction, which is the opposite of how it is
usually drawn.

Deleting the male-used acceptor of *transformer* makes the female-specific
acceptor fire with no Sex-lethal activity at all. What Sxl does is block the
default site rather than switch on the female one
[@tra1989splicesiteblockage]. The block is competitive occupancy of a splicing
signal. Sxl binds the polypyrimidine tract of the non-sex-specific acceptor and
keeps U2AF off it, which leaves U2AF free to activate the weaker female-specific
acceptor instead [@sxl1993u2afantagonism].

At the bottom of the chain the activators are unusually strong rather than
typical. Measured by quantitative kinetics, Tra, Tra2 and 9G8 recruit the
spliceosome far more effectively than other SR-family proteins, and more
effectively than their serine-arginine content predicts
[@sciabica2006traactivators].

A chemical mark on the RNA contributes as well. Female flies mutant for either
of the two m6A methyltransferase subunits *ime4* or *mettl14* accumulated both
the male and the female Sxl isoform in heads, instead of the female one alone
[@kan2017m6asexdetermination]. How much the switch leans on the m6A reader shows
only under stress. With one wild-type copy of *Sxl* removed, homozygotes for the
strong YT521-B allele NP3 produced just 16 per cent of the expected number of
surviving adult females, against 74 and 71 per cent for two weaker alleles
[@kan2017m6asexdetermination].

### A loop that remembers which decision was made

A developmental switch has to hold its position after the signal that set it has
gone. In this cascade the memory is a splicing loop, and the loop is the part of
the system an earlier draft of this chapter asserted without evidence.

Sex-lethal drives the splicing of its own transcript. Expressing a female *Sxl*
cDNA in transgenic males switched splicing from the male to the female pattern
and trans-activated the endogenous gene, which closes a loop in which Sxl
protein causes more Sxl protein to be made [@sxl1991positiveautoregulation]. The
two states are then held by different means. The female state is kept by that
autoregulation, while the male state is what the default machinery produces when
no Sxl protein is present [@sxl1991positiveautoregulation].

Autoregulation does not reuse the mechanism Sxl applies to *transformer*.
Skipping the male exon of *Sxl* requires several cis elements both upstream and
downstream of that exon, sitting too far from the splice sites for direct
competition. Regulation acts mainly on the exon's 5' splice site rather than
its 3' [@sxl1993autoregulationciselements].

What that architecture buys is a threshold. A stochastic model built on the
measured molecular details gives all-or-none bistable behaviour, so the loop
both commits the cell and remembers the commitment. A small early pulse of Sxl
protein leaves the loop switched off [@sxl2003theoreticalmodel]. That last
result is a model rather than a measurement, and is recorded here as one.

### Holding the male state takes work too

The account above makes the male state passive, a default that needs no
maintaining. A later result makes that description doubtful.

Flies of both sexes carry a paralogue that competes for the same RNA sites Sxl
uses. In gel-shift experiments the RNA-binding domains of Sxl and of
Sister-of-Sex-lethal bound a uridine-rich element one at a time rather than
together, and either protein could displace the other
[@moschall2018ssx]. Removing that competitor lets the switch leak. Roughly 5 per
cent of males hemizygous for a transposon insertion in *ssx* produced *Sxl*
messages lacking the poison exon, which encode functional protein
[@moschall2018ssx].

The leak stops short of the phenotype, since splicing of the downstream target
*transformer* stayed male in those animals [@moschall2018ssx]. So the male state
is actively guarded at the top of the cascade and buffered further down, which is
a more robust arrangement than a bare default and a less tidy one.

### The memory sits elsewhere in other insects

The cascade is often presented as the insect sex-determination pathway. It is
better described as one arrangement of a conserved bottom half.

On the tephritid model, *transformer* rather than *Sex-lethal* holds the state
through an autoregulatory function. A comparative survey of twelve
*Anastrepha* species led those authors to conclude that this arrangement was
likely already present in the common ancestor of three tephritid genera
[@ruiz2007traanastrepha]. In the honeybee the regulator may be what sharpens the
decision rather than what makes it. Am-Tra2 is required for the female splice of
*fem*, and is proposed also to push *fem* toward the non-productive male form
when heteroallelic Csd protein is absent, a double role its authors read as
stabilising the binary outcome [@nissen2012amtra2].

That system also gives a direct demonstration that the splice choice carries the
decision. Injecting 4 picograms of double-stranded RNA against *Am-tra2* per
embryo produced male-spliced *Am-dsx* message in females, a product entirely
absent from control embryos, which made only the female form
[@nissen2012amtra2].

## Sex determination in humans: WT1 and three amino acids {#sec-wt1}

The fly cascade is a switch demonstrated by genetics. The clearest human case
has a different character, because the evidence runs from a mutation that shifts
an isoform ratio to a phenotype, with the direction of causation established in
mouse afterwards.

*WT1* uses two donor sites at one position, and the choice inserts or omits three
amino acids. Inserting lysine, threonine and serine between the last two zinc
fingers abolishes DNA binding and sends the protein to nuclear speckles. The
shorter form acts as a transcriptional activator or repressor depending on
context [@gregoire2023ktsovarian]. Three residues out of a protein of several
hundred change what the molecule binds.

### Frasier syndrome shifts a ratio without losing a protein

Frasier syndrome is a splicing defect rather than a lost protein. Intronic point
mutations at the exon 9 donor site stop the mutant allele from making the
normally more abundant +KTS form. No mutant protein is produced, which those
authors contrast with Denys-Drash syndrome, where the mutations are heterozygous
and dominant-negative [@wt11998frasierktsratio].

The shift has been measured in a patient. In a boy with focal segmental
glomerulosclerosis and genital anomalies carrying the 1228+4 C-to-T mutation, the
+KTS to -KTS transcript ratio was 0.43, against 1.50 to 2.00 in healthy controls
[@wt12000splicesiterarefsgs]. He was the only such carrier among 37 children
screened [@wt12000splicesiterarefsgs], so the denominator here is one patient
rather than a series.

### The mouse experiments make the ratio causal

A human ratio measured alongside a human phenotype leaves the direction of
causation open. The mouse work settles the direction of causation.

Raising -KTS to the level seen in Frasier syndrome made ovaries differentiate
early regardless of the embryo's genetic sex. In XY embryos it suppressed
*Sry* and produced male-to-female sex reversal, while losing -KTS blocked gonadal
differentiation altogether [@gregoire2023ktsovarian]. That is an isoform ratio
determining which gonad an embryo builds.

Two further results from the same work sharpen what the ratio is doing. The
gene's output changed composition rather than falling, since the knockout gonads
held twice the -KTS message that controls did, while their total WT1 protein was
no different [@gregoire2023ktsovarian]. This is a case where dosage of the gene
is held constant and only the mix changes, which is the distinction
@sec-how-functional turns on.

Within that shift the active ingredient is the level of one isoform rather than
the absence of the other. Embryos lacking +KTS but carrying one -KTS allele had
more SRY-positive cells than embryos lacking +KTS with two -KTS alleles, so *Sry*
is suppressed in proportion to how much -KTS is present and does not require
+KTS at all [@gregoire2023ktsovarian].

### A counter-case the ratio model does not explain

Two findings sit outside the account above, and neither has been resolved in
this book's corpus.

The ratio is not necessary for the syndrome. Two unrelated patients with Frasier
syndrome carried new mutations in *WT1* exon 9 that left the +KTS to -KTS ratio
unaltered, in the same exon where Denys-Drash mutations occur, which led those
authors to treat the two syndromes as one condition
[@wt11999exon9nonratio]. What those mutations do instead is not stated in the
material available here.

And the phenotype is sex-specific in a way the ratio alone does not predict. Two
sisters carrying identical *WT1* intron 9 mutations differed in outcome. The
46,XY proband had Frasier syndrome with gonadal dysgenesis, while her 46,XX
sister had the same progressive kidney disease with entirely normal female
development [@wt11999frasiersisters]. One molecular lesion produced a kidney
phenotype in both and a gonadal phenotype in only one. Whatever the ratio does,
it acts on a substrate that already differs between the two.

Not every splicing mutation in a sex-development gene works this way, and the
distinction matters for how such cases are counted. In a 46,XY patient the
*NR5A1* change c.244G>T was predicted to be a missense substitution but left
transcriptional activity intact. A minigene assay showed it instead deletes
exon 2 or 19 nucleotides of it [@yu2021nr5a1splicing]. That is a
loss-of-function splicing defect rather than an isoform-ratio case, and only the
second kind bears on this chapter's argument.

## CD45: a switch on T cell activation {#sec-cd45}

A developmental cascade sets an isoform once and leaves it. CD45 runs comparable
machinery repeatedly, as routine immune function, and the evidence for what the
switch achieves is thinner than the evidence that it happens.

Human CD45 makes five transmembrane phosphatase isoforms differing only in their
extracellular domains, by including or skipping variable exons 4, 5 and 6.
Resting T cells carry long forms retaining two or three of those exons.
Activated T cells drop most or all of them [@cd452005variableexonelements].

What is conserved in that extracellular region is its shape rather than any
binding site. Sequence identity across mammalian CD45 ectodomains is under 15
per cent, against over 90 per cent for the ectodomains of type II receptor
phosphatases. The conservation that does exist falls at the interfaces between
domains rather than on any surface likely to bind a ligand
[@chang2016cd45segregation]. That is the profile of a molecule selected for how
far it holds something from the membrane.

Direct measurement of the ectodomains supports that reading. Isolated
ectodomains of both the long and the short isoform, anchored to a supported
lipid bilayer, held their N-terminal tags further from the surface than the
distance spanned by a T cell receptor bound to its ligand
[@chang2016cd45segregation]. Both forms are tall enough to be excluded from a
close contact, which is the usual explanation for why length should matter at
all.

### The ectodomain's effect on signalling is disputed

An earlier draft of this chapter stated that the short isoform supports antigen
recognition best, and that the splice choice tunes signalling sensitivity. The
first half has a primary behind it, and so do three results pointing the other
way.

The supporting result: in T cell lines carrying a defined receptor, the short
exon-null isoform characteristic of memory CD4 cells supported antigen
recognition best [@cd451994isoformsrecognition]. An isoform comparison published
the same year runs the other way. Raising CD45RABC, the long form of resting
cells, increased CD4 thymic T cell proliferation, calcium mobilisation and
phosphotyrosine. CD45R0 did neither and needed a second stimulus even to
raise proliferation [@cd451994specificisoforms].

Shortening the ectodomain does not simply raise signalling. A chimeric CD45
carrying the large ectodomain of CD43 restored receptor signalling in CD45-null
T cells, while chimeras carrying small ectodomains from other phosphatases did
not. Both resting Lck activity and the receptor-induced rise in zeta-chain
phosphorylation required a CD45 with a large ectodomain
[@cd452003ectodomaingems].

Two experiments then suggest the variable that matters is amount rather than
identity. Transgenic mice expressed only CD45RABC or only CD45R0 on a CD45-null
background. T cell development and peripheral function, tested by influenza and
lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus challenge, tracked the amount of CD45 rather
than which isoform supplied it [@cd452004tgisoformlevel]. Comparing
CD45RO, CD45RB and CD45RABC transgenes directly, all three gave CD4 T cell
hyper-reactivity at intermediate expression, so that effect follows dose rather
than splice form [@cd452008isoformindependent].

The mechanism usually invoked to explain why length should matter also has a
timing problem. On bilayers presenting a high-affinity anti-CD3 single-chain
antibody elongated with a CD43 stalk, CD45 was still largely colocalised with
receptor microclusters at one minute and only partly segregated between three
and ten minutes. A length-matched low-affinity ligand that cannot activate T
cells kept CD45 colocalised throughout [@alaghbar2018cd45segregation]. On that
evidence phosphatase exclusion can follow receptor triggering rather than cause
it.

The defensible statement is narrower than the one this chapter used to make. The
splice choice changes the ectodomain, the ectodomain is built to set a height,
and what that height does to signalling is contested, with at least one strand
of evidence suggesting the dominant variable is how much CD45 is present.

### hnRNPLL drives the switch, and costimulation induces it

The regulation is better settled than the function, and it answers a question
this chapter previously left open: what makes the switch run in one direction.

A short-hairpin screen picked out hnRNPLL as a critical inducible regulator.
Levels of it climbed on stimulation, it attached to CD45 message, and it proved
both necessary and sufficient for the switch. Depletion and overexpression moved
CD45RA and CD45RO in opposite directions [@cd452008hnrnpllregulation]. It is the
major repressor of the variable exons, acting through two CA elements in exon 6,
and its action is combinatorial rather than exon-by-exon
[@preussner2012hnrnplcd45]. The three variable exons are not controlled as a
unit: in cells carrying a minigene with all three, hnRNP L repressed only exon
4, hnRNP LL repressed exons 4 and 6. Exon 5 was never repressed on its own by
either protein [@preussner2012hnrnplcd45].

The repressor is induced rather than constitutive, and costimulation sets the
pace. In sorted naive mouse CD4 T cells, hnRNPLL message stayed low with
anti-CD3 alone and rose about twofold by 12 hours and about fivefold by 24 hours
when anti-CD28 costimulation was added [@butte2012cd28splicing]. The protein
followed the same pattern: negligible in unstimulated cells and detected only at
72 hours with anti-CD3 alone, but present by 24 hours with costimulation, higher
by 48 and sustained at 72 [@butte2012cd28splicing].

Deranging the switch is not sufficient for a phenotype, which is a useful
control on how much to read into it. Mice carrying a point mutation in hnRNPLL
failed to silence *Ptprc* exons 4 to 6 and their plasmablasts could not
downregulate B220. B cell development, mature B cell numbers, proliferation
to receptor and Toll-like receptor stimuli, and plasmablast generation were all
normal [@hnrnpll2021bcellnoimpact].

### The switch runs backwards as well

Calling the switch reversible needs evidence that it returns, and that evidence
is recent.

After live attenuated yellow fever vaccination, cells recognising one epitope
were 21 per cent CD45RA positive at two weeks and 51.5 per cent at four weeks.
Cells recognising a second epitope went from 22.5 per cent to 44.4 per cent over
the same interval [@mcguire2025cd45reexpression]. Withdrawing antigen is
what drives the return. Sorted CD45RO effector CD8 T cells from vaccinees held
CD45RO when cultured with their peptide. Without it 20 to 70 per cent
re-expressed CD45RA within four days, and hnRNP LL message was higher in the
peptide-stimulated cells [@mcguire2025cd45reexpression].

So the cycle closes, which the fly cascade's does not. One proposed human
consequence of the switch does not hold up, though. The silent 77C-to-G change
in CD45 exon 4, reported to raise CD45RA expression in carriers, was found in 10
of 347 controls and 7 of 454 multiple sclerosis patients, with no association
overall and none within clinical or HLA-DRB1*15 subgroups
[@miterski2002ptprcms].

## Bcl-x: two products that oppose each other

The *bcl-x* locus was described from the outset as making two products that pull
against each other, with the short form actively opposing bcl-2 rather than
merely failing to protect cells [@bclx1993dominantregulator].

Bcl-xS lacks 63 amino acids spanning the conserved BH1 and BH2 regions, which is
the stretch that makes Bcl-xL most resemble Bcl-2 [@bclx1996santagonizesl]. The
functional reversal reduces to one deleted block.

### Two primaries disagree about the mechanism

The antagonism between the two products is settled. How it works has been
answered twice, in opposite directions, and an earlier draft of this chapter
reported the disagreement incorrectly by saying no primary report supported the
heterodimer model.

The report that established the antagonism argued against that model. Bcl-xS
bound Bcl-xL only weakly in vitro compared with Bax, coimmunoprecipitation from
mammalian cells showed no detectable heterodimers with other family members.
Overexpressing Bcl-xS left Bax able to heterodimerise with Bcl-xL in vivo
[@bclx1996santagonizesl]. Three years later the same question was answered the
other way. Bcl-xS did form heterodimers with Bcl-xL in mammalian cells, its
ability to block survival tracked its ability to heterodimerise, and deletion
mutants retaining an intact BH3 domain kept that ability
[@bclx1999bh3heterodimer]. A 2019 review states the mechanism as direct
inhibition [@stevens2019bclxsplicing], which repeats the second of those results
rather than resting on nothing.

What happens downstream is better established than the first step. In mouse
embryonic fibroblasts deficient in Bax, Bak, Apaf-1 or caspase-9, Bak but not
Bax proved essential for Bcl-xS-induced apoptosis [@bclx2005bakessential]. How
the short isoform reaches Bak was then answered without direct contact between
them. In melanoma cells Bcl-xS coimmunoprecipitated reciprocally with the
channel protein VDAC2 but showed no direct interaction with Bak, and
overexpressing VDAC2 strongly reduced the killing [@bclx2012vdac2bak].

Two decades of work on one isoform pair have produced a settled phenotype, a
settled downstream requirement, and a first step still argued over. All four of
those reports were read here as abstracts, which is a limit on how finely the
disagreement can be characterised.

## Titin: splicing sets cardiac stiffness

Titin is the case where a spliced product's physical properties are the
phenotype. The adult human heart runs a long compliant N2BA form of roughly
3,200 to 3,500 kDa alongside a short stiff N2B form near 3,000 kDa. Both are
spliced from one gene of 364 exons [@li2022rbm20titinstiffness]. The difference
comes down to how much extensible material survives splicing. The compliant form
keeps more PEVK and immunoglobulin-like spring elements in the I-band.

RBM20 is the principal regulator of titin pre-mRNA, and losing a single
functional copy shifts splicing toward highly compliant isoforms and degrades
the Frank-Starling response [@li2022rbm20titinstiffness].
A splice-factor dose change is sufficient to alter cardiac mechanics.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why a spliced-out segment changes stiffness

Titin spans half a sarcomere and sits in series with the contractile machinery
like a spring. Its I-band region holds tandem immunoglobulin-like domains that
unfold under load, plus a PEVK segment behaving as an entropic spring. Keeping
more of those elements lengthens the spring, so the same stretch produces less
restoring force. Splicing here sets how much polymer sits between two anchors
instead of tuning an enzyme's activity.
:::

## FGFR: one exon pair decides the ligand {#sec-fgfr}

In FGFR1 through FGFR3, the mutually exclusive IIIb and IIIc exons encode the
C-terminal half of immunoglobulin loop III, which sits in the ligand-binding
site. The splice choice determines which fibroblast growth factors the receptor
can respond to at all [@holzmann2011fgfrigiiisplicing].

Deleting IIIb in mouse is lethal, while deleting IIIc instead produces skeletal
malformations [@holzmann2011fgfrigiiisplicing], so the two forms are not
interchangeable.

How absolute the discrimination is has been measured for one ligand pair. FGF7
and FGF10 activate only the IIIb form of FGFR2. The crystal structure of FGFR2b
bound to FGF10 traces that to contacts between divergent regions of FGF10 and
two loops specific to the IIIb exon, with a rotation of the second
immunoglobulin domain adding further contacts [@fgfr2003structuralspecificity].
No comparable matrix across the rest of the family appears in this book's
corpus. The general claim that the switch repartitions ligand responsiveness
rests on a small number of measured pairs.

### ESRP1 and ESRP2 make the choice

Both regulators have been identified, and how they behave with respect to dose
is unusual enough to be worth stating precisely, because the picture in cultured
cells and the picture in the animal are not the same.

In cultured cells the choice can be driven either way by one pair of proteins.
Expressing either ESRP1 or ESRP2 in cells making FGFR2-IIIc switched endogenous
splicing to the epithelial IIIb form. Knocking both down in cells making
FGFR2-IIIb switched it to the mesenchymal form [@esrp2009fgfr2regulators].

In the animal the same pair behaves as a threshold rather than a dial. Across
nine genotype combinations, mouse epidermal Fgfr2-IIIb splicing did not shift at
all until both *Esrp1* and *Esrp2* were deleted, so a single copy of *Esrp2*
holds it. In the double knockout, Fgfr1, Fgfr2 and Fgfr3 each switched
completely to the IIIc form [@bebee2015esrpprogram].

The two paralogues are not equivalent in the animal. Mice with a germline
*Esrp1* knockout were born with clefts of the lip and palate on both sides, in
every one of more than forty embryos examined, and died the day they were born.
*Esrp2*-null mice were viable and fertile with no detectable abnormality
[@bebee2015esrpprogram]. The same factor is needed to build a kidney.
Three-dimensional reconstruction of serially sectioned E13.5 embryos counted
34.25 plus or minus 7.27 developing glomeruli in four *Esrp1*-null kidneys,
against 49.75 plus or minus 7.13 in four wild-type littermates. That is 69 per
cent of control at p equal to 0.0227 [@bebee2016esrp1kidney].

### The tumour evidence points both ways

Usage splits by compartment, with IIIb forms in epithelia and IIIc forms in
mesenchyme. A IIIb-to-IIIc switch in an epithelial tumour is associated with
increased invasiveness in bladder and prostate cancer
[@holzmann2011fgfrigiiisplicing].

A large prostate series complicates that for one of those tissues. On a tissue
microarray, nuclear ESRP1 staining was seen in 38.6 per cent of 12,140
interpretable cancers and nuclear ESRP2 in 41.9 per cent of 12,962. High
staining for either went with advanced tumour stage, high Gleason grade, lymph
node metastasis and early PSA recurrence, each at p below 0.0001
[@freytag2020esrpprostate]. High ESRP is the condition under which the
epithelial IIIb form is made, so that association runs opposite to the
IIIb-to-IIIc account.

The two results are not strictly contradictory, because the prostate study
measured the splicing factors by immunohistochemistry and never measured FGFR2
isoforms. It does mean the direction of the switch in prostate cancer should not
be stated from splicing-factor levels alone.

## PKM: the switch tumours do not make

Pyruvate kinase M is the textbook illustration of how much can ride on one
mutually exclusive exon pair. It is also the clearest case of an isoform story
outrunning its evidence, which is why it belongs here.

Antisense oligonucleotides blocking an exon 10 enhancer, forcing exon 9
inclusion, killed glioblastoma cells. The authors attribute the death to loss of
PK-M2 rather than to gain of PK-M1 [@wang2012pkmantisense].

The familiar version goes further and holds that tumours switch from PKM1 to
PKM2. Absolute mass spectrometry across 25 human cancers with tissue-matched
controls found PKM2 predominant in tumours and equally predominant in the
matched normal tissue, and those authors reject the switch
[@bluemlein2011pkmnoshift].

### Four experiments, four different signs

Deleting the tumour-associated isoform in mouse has now been done in several
tissues, and the results do not agree on a direction.

In mice carrying conditional *Apc* and *Pkm2* alleles, the fraction developing
one or more colon tumours was no different with or without PKM2 at three weeks,
at six weeks or later. PKM2 loss also left overall survival and nuclear
beta-catenin staining unchanged [@lau2017pkm2colon]. The same null result holds
in a second tumour type and a different driver genotype: in a *Kras* and *Trp53*
model of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, deletion of *Pkm2* changed neither
overall survival nor tumour size. PKM1 appeared in its place without altering
the number of proliferating cells [@hillis2018pkm2pdac].

In one tissue the deletion pushed the phenotype the opposite way. Deleting
*Pkm2* in Lgr5-positive intestinal stem cells significantly increased both the
incidence and the size of colon tumours in a colitis-associated model, compared
with vehicle-treated animals of the same genotype [@kim2019pkm2colitis].

Forcing the splice choice has a large phenotype in a cell line, tumours do not
make the switch. Removing the isoform in vivo gives no effect twice and a
protective effect once. The lesson from this gene generalises past it. A
phenotype that follows from forcing an isoform ratio in culture does not
establish that the ratio is doing that job where it occurs naturally.

## Two more cases at a ligand-binding surface

The FGFR pattern, where a small alternative segment sits in a binding surface
and changes what the protein will respond to, is not unique to that family. Two
further cases are worth stating because the evidence in each reaches a different
depth.

### A splice insert that selects a receptor class

Neurexins carry an alternatively spliced segment at splice site 4, and switching
it changes which postsynaptic receptor responds.

Conditional knockin mice that switch the segment on and off showed the insert in
neurexin-1 raising NMDA receptor currents without touching AMPA receptor
currents, the insert in neurexin-3 suppressing AMPA currents without touching
NMDA currents. The insert in neurexin-2 doing neither, with synapse density
unchanged throughout [@neurexin2019ss4receptors]. Three closely related proteins
carrying the same insert therefore do three different things with it, and one
does nothing measurable.

The mechanism is recruitment of a secreted partner rather than a change to the
synapse itself. Deleting cerebellin-2 completely abolished the effect of the
presynaptic neurexin-1 and neurexin-3 splice variants on NMDA and AMPA receptor
currents at CA1-to-subiculum synapses. None of these manipulations altered
paired-pulse ratios, so release probability was untouched
[@dai2022neurexincerebellin].

### A risk allele that shifts a ratio

The interleukin-7 receptor supplies a case where a common human variant changes
a splice choice. Where the size of the effect has been measured and then
reversed in culture.

A polymorphism inside the alternatively spliced exon 6 of *IL7R* was associated
with multiple sclerosis across four independent family-based or case-control
datasets at a combined p of 2.9 times ten to the minus seven. It shifts the
balance between the soluble and membrane-bound forms of the receptor
[@il7r2007mssplicing]. In reporter cell lines differing only at that variant,
exon 6 was skipped in 78.2 per cent of transcripts with the risk allele against
57.2 per cent with the protective allele. Two antisense oligonucleotides
brought the risk-allele line to 44.3 and 62.8 per cent
[@galarzamunoz2022il7raso].

The genetic half of that story has not held everywhere. A case-control study of
200 patients and 200 healthy controls found no association between the exon 6
variant and disease. A promoter variant in the same gene was significantly
associated, and those authors describe their result as contrary to earlier
reports [@il7r2014promoternotsplicing]. That study is small beside the four
datasets behind the original association. It is recorded here because a single
non-replication is part of the evidence rather than a footnote to it.

## fruitless: one splice choice specifies a behaviour

The strongest sufficiency experiment in this chapter concerns a behaviour rather
than a cell or a tissue.

Alleles of *fruitless* locked into the male or the female splice form showed
that male splicing is necessary for male courtship and sexual orientation. That
it is sufficient to make otherwise normal female flies court other females
[@fru2005splicingcourtship]. The splice form rather than the chromosomal sex
predicts the behaviour, which is as direct a demonstration as this chapter
contains that an isoform choice can be the decision.

### Three isoforms within the male programme

Inside that programme the isoforms are not interchangeable either. Most
*fruitless*-expressing cells make all three alternative zinc-finger isoforms, yet
the strongest behavioural impairment came from losing FruC, whose mutants failed
to copulate and lacked sine song. The sexually dimorphic cell shapes depended
on FruC rather than on any other single isoform
[@vonphilipsborn2014fruisoforms]. A repertoire can be both redundant in
expression and non-redundant in function.

## Splicing regulators as developmental switches

In the cases above the isoform is the unit of interest. A related body of work
changes the regulator instead, and it bears on this chapter with one caveat
attached. Deleting a splicing factor changes many targets at once, so a
phenotype belongs to the programme rather than to any single isoform.

Three results show how far that approach reaches. CRISPR removal of the elements
controlling *Pbx1* exon 7 in mouse embryonic stem cells forced expression of the
neuronal Pbx1a isoform and switched on transcription of neuronal genes
[@linares2015ptbp1pbx1]. That is a cis-element deletion rather than a gene
deletion, which puts it closer to an isoform experiment. Ablating *Esrp1* gave
cleft lip and palate, and removing *Esrp2* as well produced widespread
developmental defects including failure to build a skin barrier
[@bebee2015esrpprogram]. And two highly homologous regulators are not
equivalent in vivo: mice lacking *Nova2* had no corpus callosum and specific
axon outgrowth failures in ventral motoneurons, while mice lacking *Nova1* did
not [@saito2016nova2axon].

## How much of this is functional {#sec-how-functional}

Three bodies of evidence bear on whether most alternative splicing resembles the
cases above, and they disagree in an informative way.

The 2008 tissue survey identified over 22,000 tissue-specific alternative
transcript events and estimated that 52 to 80 per cent of events of each type
are tissue-regulated [@wang2008alternative]. Exons switching most sharply
between tissues were also likeliest to preserve reading frame in both isoforms,
read by those authors as splicing making two intact proteins rather than
switching a gene off [@wang2008alternative].

Most of the catalogue is not conserved. A human-mouse comparison predicted only
about 2,000 conserved alternatively spliced exons, and found them markedly more
frame-preserving and domain-sparing than the rest. Those authors concluded that
the great majority of alternative splicing in the human EST record has no mouse
counterpart [@conservedas2005humanmouseexons]. The same split appears in
invertebrates, where splicing events differing between *C. elegans* tissues are
preferentially frame-preserving and better conserved across *Caenorhabditis*
than other alternative exons [@koterniak2020celegansplicing].

Some of it is error, and some is neither error nor protein diversity. De novo
junction discovery found about 150,000 previously unannotated junctions in human
cells, with little conservation at the new splice sites. The implied error rate
was near 0.7 per cent per intron, and lower in highly expressed genes
[@pickrell2010noisysplicing]. One transcript usually dominates, with roughly 85
per cent of protein-coding mRNA in primary tissues coming from each gene's major
transcript. About 35 per cent of genes switch which transcript dominates between
tissues, and those authors declined to call minor transcripts functionless
[@gonzalezporta2013dominanttranscript].

A third position comes from measuring unproductive splicing across eight assays,
which gave threefold more of it than steady-state RNA had suggested, with 15 per
cent of transcript molecules from protein-coding genes unproductive. In
the same work, trait-associated loci acting through splicing were as often
explained by decay-driven expression changes as by isoform usage
[@fair2024unproductivesplicing]. On that account, much alternative splicing acts
as a volume control, and @sec-as-nmd gives the mechanism.

The three results fit together once a single answer stops being expected. Most
splicing events are rare, unconserved and probably inconsequential. A minority
are switch-like, frame-preserving and conserved, and a further portion sets
expression level through decay. Every case earlier in this chapter comes from
the second group. Nothing here licenses treating an annotated isoform as a
functional entity merely because it is annotated.

One distinction runs through every case in this chapter and is worth naming
before the chapter closes. Several of the examples above turn on a change in the
*mix* of isoforms while the total output of the gene stays put. The WT1 mouse
work established that directly, and the Dscam1 docking-site alleles were built
to isolate it. Others turn out, on examination, to be changes in how much
protein is present, which is the reading two CD45 transgene experiments support
and the one the PKM deletions are hardest to escape. A gene-level measurement
cannot tell those apart, and neither can a sentence that says a gene is
"alternatively spliced in disease". The question is always whether the mix
changed, and whether the mix changing is what did the work.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The 95 per cent figure and its denominators

Two 2008 papers put alternative splicing at roughly 95 per cent of human
multi-exon genes, and the number now circulates stripped of its conditions.

Extrapolating by read coverage gave about 98 per cent of multi-exon genes
excluding cell lines, and about 100 per cent using all samples. Requiring a minor
isoform to reach 15 per cent frequency in at least one sample drops it to 92 per
cent of multi-exon genes, or roughly 86 per cent of all human genes
[@wang2008alternative]. The independent survey reached about 95 per cent of
multi-exon genes by a different route, and counted about 100,000 intermediate- to
high-abundance splicing events in major tissues [@pan2008deepsurveying].

Three things vary between those statements: whether the denominator is multi-exon
genes or all genes, what abundance threshold a minor isoform must clear, and
whether detection is direct or extrapolated. Quoted without them, "95 per cent"
is uninterpretable rather than wrong.
:::
